subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Fold, Share, and Find the Half

tasks_in_class.description: Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen (half or two quarters) and why; try with paper; reason about equal division and Samina's choice.
Colour the figures that Samina has divided into halves correctly; explain how you got the answer.
Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.

time_bands.activity: Each pair of students folds a rectangular sheet of paper to find a half; they compare their fold with a neighbour's and discuss whether both pieces look equal. The teacher asks: 'How do you know these are really equal?' and invites students to try overlapping the two pieces to check.

Let Us Discuss Q1–4, p.62 ("Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen....") — Teacher reads the Ikra and Samina scenario aloud; small groups discuss which piece they would choose and why. Groups share their reasoning: is a half really the same as two quarters? Students test their claim by folding paper.

Let Us Do Q1, p.63 ("Colour the figures that Samina has divided into halves....") — Students work individually, colouring and explaining their choices. Teacher circulates and asks: 'How can you tell the two parts are equal?' followed by Let Us Do Q2, p.63 ("Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.") where students draw their own dividing lines.

Whole-class share-out: two or three students show their divided shapes under the teacher's document camera or on the board. Class agrees or challenges whether each line truly makes equal halves. Teacher draws out the key idea — a half means two parts that are exactly the same size.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse any two-part division with a half; watch for children who draw a diagonal or off-centre line and still call each part a half. Encourage the physical overlay test — placing one part on top of the other — as the check for equal size. Paper folding is the anchor move here: let students fold first, then draw.
materials: Rectangular sheets of paper (at least one per student)

section_titles: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters

tasks_in_class.description: Fold/cut a rectangular paper into two equal parts in as many different ways as you can; try with actual paper.
Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts (1/4 or quarter).
Match the given part-shapes (hourglass, triangle, semicircle, rectangle) with their corresponding whole shapes using the 1/2 and 1/4 labels.

homework.description: Divide the given shapes (diamond, rectangle, oval, L-shape, cross-shape) into 4 equal parts/quarters.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Try Q1, p.64 ("Fold/cut a rectangular paper into two equal parts....") — Students fold a fresh rectangle into halves in as many different ways as they can discover. Pairs compare folds and display distinct solutions on the desk. Teacher prompts: 'Are there more ways? Can you fold diagonally and still get equal parts?'

Let Us Try Q2, p.65 ("Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts....") — Students now work with a second sheet, folding it into quarters in different ways, then sketch each fold pattern in their notebooks. Teacher introduces the word 'quarter' and writes 1/4 on the board, connecting it to the four equal parts the students just made.

Let Us Try Q3, p.65 ("Match the given part-shapes... with their corresponding whole shapes....") — Students examine printed part-shapes and reason about which whole each could have come from. They discuss: 'If this is one quarter, what does the whole look like?' Class shares matches and explains their thinking.

Quick whole-class close: teacher holds up two differently-folded quarters of the same rectangle and asks students to confirm both represent 1/4. Students give a thumbs-up or thumbs-down and explain briefly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly assume a rectangle can only be halved horizontally or vertically; the diagonal fold surprises many and opens the idea that the same fraction can look different. The matching task at the end is a good diagnostic — a student who cannot reverse from part to whole is still thinking of the fraction as a picture rather than a relationship. Let students trace and fold rather than just draw, as the kinesthetic step matters.
materials: Rectangular sheets of paper (two per student)
Printed part-shape cards or textbook page 65

section_titles: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
periods.activity_title: Sharing the Dhokla — Smaller Pieces, Bigger Crowd

tasks_in_class.description: Observe Sumedha's share as each guest arrives; reason about 9 vs 11 people; how many 1/6 pieces make a whole; Sumedha's share if two guests give theirs back.
How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people? Who gets bigger pieces? Draw and explain.
Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people; discuss why fractions get smaller as people increase.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the dhokla story: one round dhokla is to be shared equally. Students cut a circular piece of paper (or fold it) to show one half, one third, and one quarter. The teacher posts the three circles on the board and invites students to compare the pieces physically.

Let Us Discuss Q1–4, p.68 ("Observe Sumedha's share as each guest arrives....") — Teacher narrates the guest-arrival story while students act it out with their paper circles. For each new guest, they fold again and discuss: 'Is Sumedha's piece bigger or smaller now?' The question about 9 vs 11 people is posed to groups who debate before sharing.

Let Us Do Q1, p.68 ("How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people?....") — Students draw circles divided into 6 and 8 parts respectively, shade one part of each, and write the fraction. They compare the two shaded pieces and explain in a sentence who gets more.

Let Us Do Q2, p.69 ("Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people....") — Students shade pre-drawn circles for each case and lay them in order from largest share to smallest. Class discusses: 'What happens to the piece as the number of people grows?'

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error at this stage is believing that a larger number in the fraction always means a larger piece — children say 1/8 is more than 1/3 because 8 is more than 3. Use the shaded circles side-by-side to make the visual argument before any symbolic statement. The physical fold or cut is more convincing than words here.
materials: Circular paper discs (at least three per student)

section_titles: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
periods.activity_title: Fraction Kit — Comparing and Combining Unit Fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Use fraction kit to share observations about pieces and wholes; compare two pieces; verify that 5 pieces of 1/5 make a whole; explain why a given piece is one-third.
Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4; compare 1/9 and 1/6; compare 1/6 and 1/8; choose a pair where one is smaller.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Discuss Q1–5, p.69 ("Use fraction kit to share observations about pieces and wholes....") — Students use the printed fraction kit strips (cut in advance or cut at the start of this unit). They lay pieces side-by-side: How many 1/5 pieces cover the whole? Can two 1/6 pieces cover one 1/3 piece? Students record observations in their notebooks and share one surprising finding with the class.

Whole-class guided comparison: teacher places a 1/6 strip and a 1/8 strip on the board. Students predict which is longer, then physically compare. The class articulates: 'Six equal pieces make the whole, so each 1/6 piece is longer than each 1/8 piece.' Two or three similar comparisons follow with student volunteers choosing the pairs.

Let Us Discuss fill-in-blanks, p.70 ("Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4....") — Students complete the comparison blanks independently, using their fraction kits as a check. Teacher collects responses on the board and resolves disagreements by returning to the physical strips.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with the dhokla-sharing story now apply that inverse-relationship insight using the fraction kit as a hands-on verifier. Watch for students who write '1/8 > 1/6' by reading the numerals alone — the strip comparison is the corrective, not a rule stated by the teacher. Keep fraction kits accessible throughout this unit so students reach for them first.
materials: Printed fraction-kit strips (1/2 through 1/10, one set per student)

tasks_in_class.description: Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of non-unit fractions using a strip of seven squares drawn on the board. Four squares are shaded and the class names the fraction together: four out of seven, written 4/7. Teacher then shows 2/7, 5/7, and 7/7, asking students what 7/7 means. Students discuss in pairs: 'What does it mean when the top and bottom numbers are the same?'

Let Us Do Q(a)(b)(c), p.71 ("Make a flower garden with 7 plots....") — Students draw three seven-plot strips in their notebooks and colour each plot according to the given fractions, using different colours or symbols for each flower type. For part (c), Mogra in 5/7 and Hibiscus in 2/7: students check that their two fractions add to 7/7 (the whole garden). Teacher circulates, checking that each strip has exactly seven equal plots.

Quick class check: teacher calls on volunteers to display one garden on the board and read out the fractions. Class verifies that all parts account for the whole garden. The teacher asks: 'If one more plot were added, would any of your fractions change?'

periods.teacher_notes: Students may draw unequal plots, making fractions impossible to verify visually; insist on equal-width strips before colouring begins. The key conceptual step is reading 3/7 as 'three equal parts out of seven equal parts of the whole' — not 'three and seven'. A student who writes 3/7 but cannot point to exactly three plots is still treating the fraction as a label rather than a count.

section_titles: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73
tasks_in_class.description: Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas (sectors marked with numbers show part size).
Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato; make another with 3/8 classic potato, 1/8 chilly paneer, 4/8 tangy tomato.
Meena has 8 diyas — divide into 4 equal groups to find 1/4; colour 2 diyas red.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Karan's dosa restaurant using a large circle drawn on the board divided into four equal sectors. Students name the fraction for each sector (1/4) and the class reads a short fraction table together from the textbook, connecting sector count to fraction notation.

Do It Yourself Q1–4, p.73 ("Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas....") — Students examine four pre-drawn dosa circles with numbered sectors and write the fraction for each topping. Teacher pauses after Q2 for a mid-check: 'Do all the topping fractions add up to one whole dosa?'

Let Us Explore, p.73 ("Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato....") — Students draw their own dosa circles, divide into the required equal parts, colour, and label each topping's fraction. They then design the second dosa (three toppings in eighths) and verify the fractions sum to 8/8.

Let Us Explore (diyas), p.73 ("Meena has 8 diyas — divide into 4 equal groups to find 1/4....") — Students draw 8 small diya symbols in a row, circle every group of 2, and identify each group as 1/4. They colour 2 diyas red and write: '1/4 of 8 = 2'. Teacher asks: 'How is this diya problem different from the dosa problem?'

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from a continuous circle (dosa) to a discrete collection (diyas) is the conceptual hinge of this unit — both represent 1/4 but the model looks completely different. Students who are comfortable with the circle may still struggle with the discrete set; drawing and circling equal groups before writing the fraction helps bridge the gap. A common error is colouring any 2 diyas rather than understanding that any group of 2 from 8 equal groups represents 1/4.

tasks_in_class.description: 12 cookies shared equally; find the fraction each child gets for 3, 6, 2, and 4 children.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75
tasks_in_class.description: 16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's; given Mohan's ribbon length, draw how long Rohan's ribbon would be.
Observe your surroundings and write two situations where fractions are used.

homework.description: Place hairbands on 1/3 of Simran's 9 school friends shown in a picture.
Draw flowers in 1/5 of each given group of pots (groups of 5, 10, 15 pots).

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1(a–d), p.74 ("12 cookies shared equally....") — Teacher draws 12 circles on the board to represent cookies and divides them into 3 equal groups as a class model for part (a). Students then solve parts (b), (c), and (d) individually by drawing equal groups and writing the fraction each child receives. Class compares answers and discusses why each child's share changes when the number of children changes.

Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75 ("16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts....") — Students draw 16 small squares, circle them into 4 equal groups, and write how many barfis are in 1/4. Teacher asks: 'How many barfis would be in 2/4? In 3/4?' Students extend their diagram to answer.

Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75 ("Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's....") — Students draw Mohan's ribbon at a given length (e.g., 4 cm), then reason: if this is 1/4, Rohan's ribbon must be four times as long. They draw Rohan's ribbon and label its length. Teacher checks that students use repeated addition or grouping, not guessing.

Try Yourself, p.75 ("Observe your surroundings and write two situations where fractions are used.") — Students look around the classroom or recall a recent experience and write two fraction sentences (e.g., '1/2 of the windows are open'). Two volunteers share; class confirms whether each is a valid fraction situation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students applying fractions to discrete collections often divide by sharing one at a time rather than making equal groups — this gives the correct answer but is slow and obscures the structure. Encourage drawing equal circles or boxes first, then distributing. The ribbon problem frequently trips students because they multiply Mohan's length by 4 rather than treating Mohan's length as the unit fraction; a number-line sketch along the ribbon helps.

periods.activity_title: Fold into Thirds — Discovering Equivalent Fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly; observe and write the fraction after each fold: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___.
Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time; fill in: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models folding a strip of paper into three equal parts and colouring one part. The class names the fraction (1/3). Teacher then folds the strip in half and asks: 'How many equal parts do we have now? How many are coloured?' Students count and the teacher writes 2/6 on the board, placing it next to 1/3.

Let Us Do Q1–6, p.76 ("Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly....") — Students follow the same process with their own strip: fold into thirds, colour one third, fold in half, record the new fraction; fold in half again, record; continue for two more folds. They write the chain: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___. Pairs compare their chains and discuss whether the coloured area changed.

Let Us Try, p.77 ("Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time....") — Students take a fresh strip, fold into halves, colour one half, then keep halving. They fill in 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___. Teacher asks the class: 'Did the coloured piece get bigger or smaller? Did the fraction change or stay the same?'
Brief class discussion: students share one equivalent pair they found (e.g., 1/3 = 4/12) and explain in their own words why two fractions that look different can name the same amount.

periods.teacher_notes: The cognitive leap here is that two fraction symbols can name the same part of the whole — this is genuinely surprising to many students. Do not introduce rules for generating equivalent fractions; let the folded paper do the work of showing the equality. Students who write 1/3 = 2/6 and then say '2/6 is bigger because the numbers are bigger' need to return to the folded strip and compare the coloured regions directly.
materials: Paper strips (at least two per student, same length)

periods.activity_title: Fraction Chart — Verifying Equivalence and Comparison

tasks_in_class.description: Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2; is 2/3 greater than 1/2; do ten 1/10 make a whole; do three 1/6 equal two 1/8; how many 1/8 make 1/4; find pieces that combine into a bigger piece.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes or displays the fraction chart (rows 1/2 through 1/10). Students study it silently and make one personal observation — they write it in their notebooks. A few observations are shared: students note patterns such as 'the 1/10 row has the smallest pieces' or 'two 1/4 pieces look the same size as one 1/2 piece.'

Let Us Discuss Q1–6, p.77 ("Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2....") — Teacher poses each question one at a time; students point to the rows on the chart, align pieces mentally or physically, then write their answer and a one-sentence explanation. Questions about 2/3 vs 1/2 and three 1/6 vs two 1/8 generate debate; students are invited to defend their answer using the chart.

Students work in pairs to find two more equivalences or comparisons of their own using the fraction chart (e.g., 'three 1/6 pieces equal one 1/2 piece'). Each pair writes their finding as a fraction equation or comparison sentence and shares with another pair for verification.
Class collects four or five student-generated equivalences on the board. Teacher highlights those that were surprising and asks: 'How did the chart help you check your guess?'

periods.teacher_notes: Students who completed the paper-folding activity on equivalent fractions bring the physical intuition that equal-looking coloured regions mean equal fractions; this unit channels that intuition into the visual chart. The comparison question 'Is 2/3 greater than 1/2?' is the hardest because 2/3 is not a unit fraction — students should align the 1/3 row (two pieces) against the 1/2 row (one piece) to see that 2/3 extends further. Do not move to symbolic rules; the chart is the authority.
materials: Printed fraction chart (1/2 through 1/10, one per student or per pair)

section_titles: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
periods.activity_title: Equal Parts or Not? — Reading and Naming Fractions in Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Bablu's squares — circle the ones cut into equal parts; write the fraction for the shaded part wherever possible.
Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims for shaded regions are correct; circle correct ones, cross out incorrect; draw lines to make parts equal if needed.
Identify the fraction of the whole that the blue parts make in each of three pattern-block pictures (hexagons, diamonds, arrow shapes).

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1, p.78 ("Bablu's squares — circle the ones cut into equal parts....") — Students examine a set of divided squares, decide which are cut into truly equal parts, and circle those. For the circled ones they write the fraction of the shaded region. Teacher pauses for a brief discussion: 'How do you decide whether the parts are equal? Can you always tell by looking?'

Let Us Do Q2, p.78 ("Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims....") — Students work through each claim, deciding whether the stated fraction matches the shaded region, circling correct ones and crossing out incorrect ones. Where parts are unequal they draw a line to correct the division. Pairs compare verdicts and discuss disagreements.

Let Us Do Q4, p.79 ("Identify the fraction of the whole that the blue parts make....") — Students examine three pattern-block pictures (hexagons, diamonds, arrow shapes) and write the fraction of the whole collection that is blue. Teacher reminds students to count all blocks first to name the whole, then count blue blocks for the numerator.
Quick review: teacher projects or draws one of the pattern-block images and asks the class to vote on the fraction. Any disagreement is resolved by counting aloud together.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'the shaded part is one of four pieces' with 'the shaded part is one-fourth' — the distinction matters only when the four pieces are equal. Emphasise the equal-parts condition before accepting any fraction name. The pattern-block task is useful because the blocks are distinct shapes; students must recognise that each block is one equal unit of the collection regardless of the shape it takes.

section_titles: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
periods.activity_title: Shade It Right — Fractions in Grid Figures and Irregular Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the fractions represented by the coloured parts in three given grid pictures (triangles in squares).
Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: teacher draws a rectangle divided into 6 equal parts on the board with 4 coloured. Students write the fraction on their slates or mini-boards. Teacher asks: 'What fraction is NOT coloured?' to establish that numerator and denominator both have meaning.

Let Us Do Q3, p.79 ("Identify the fractions represented by the coloured parts in three given grid pictures....") — Students count shaded triangles and total triangles in each grid picture, then write the fraction. Teacher circulates and asks: 'Are all triangles the same size? Does that matter?' The grid pictures use triangular cells, so students must confirm equal-sized units before counting.

Let Us Do Q5, p.79 ("Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts....") — Students work on each shape: dividing, then shading the specified fraction. The cross-shape requiring both 1/4 and 1/8 is done last. Students who finish early are invited to find a different way to shade 2/3 of the rectangle and check with a partner whether the new shading still represents 2/3.

Gallery moment: students hold up their L-shape (3/4 shaded) and do a quick peer-check across the room. Any student whose shading looks different explains their division strategy; the class decides whether it is still 3/4.

periods.teacher_notes: Dividing irregular shapes such as the L-shape or cross into equal parts is genuinely hard — students may shade three of four unequal pieces and call it 3/4. Remind them to divide first into equal parts (they may use a ruler and count squares if the shape sits on a grid), then shade. The equivalence insight from earlier paper folding — that the same fraction can look different — is revisited here: shading 4/6 of a circle and 2/3 of a rectangle both represent the same proportion, and alert students may notice this without being told.

items.section_title: Parts and Wholes — Halves
items.prompt: Draw a rectangle in your notebook. Draw a line on it to divide it into two equal halves. How do you know the two parts are equal?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any line dividing the rectangle into two parts of the same size — a horizontal, vertical, or diagonal cut through the centre — is correct. The student should state that the two parts are equal because one piece covers the other exactly (or they are the same size).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold or overlap the two parts to check that they match exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold the rectangle first, then trace the fold line; stretch: ask them to show a second, different line that also makes two equal halves.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: Below is a square. Show two different ways to divide it into four equal parts (quarters). Draw the dividing lines for each way.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two distinct sets of lines that divide the square into four equal parts are correct — for example, two horizontal cuts, one horizontal and one vertical, or diagonal cuts through the centre. Each resulting piece must be the same size.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the square into four parts and verify each part is the same size by overlapping or counting equal sub-units.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a paper square and trace the creases; stretch: ask them to find a third different way and explain how they know all four parts are equal.

exercise.description: Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts (1/4 or quarter).

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: A rectangle is divided into four parts. Which description tells you that each part is one quarter (1/4)?

options.label: A
options.text: The four parts are all different shapes and sizes.

options.label: B
options.text: The four parts are all the same size.

options.label: C
options.text: The rectangle has four sides.

options.label: D
options.text: The rectangle is divided into four parts with one part shaded.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The four parts are all the same size.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A quarter means one of four equal parts; equality of size is the defining condition for naming any part a fraction.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not yet connected 'quarter' with the requirement of equal parts — they see four parts but ignore the equal-size condition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates the act of shading (identifying a part) with the definition of a quarter — shading does not create equal parts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is associating the number four with the shape's property (four sides) rather than the number of equal parts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a paper rectangle into four parts and compare pieces; stretch: ask them to draw an example where a rectangle is cut into four parts that are NOT quarters.

exercise.description: Fold/cut a rectangular paper into two equal parts in as many different ways as you can; try with actual paper.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: Draw a circle. Divide it to show the share each person gets when 5 people share one roti equally. Shade one person's share and write the fraction.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The circle is divided into 5 equal parts; one part is shaded. The fraction is 1/5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the circle into as many equal parts as there are people; shade one part and write 1 over the number of parts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a circle already divided into 5 equal parts and ask them to shade and name one part; stretch: ask them to shade 3 parts and name that fraction.

exercise.description: Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people; discuss why fractions get smaller as people increase.

items.section_title: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
items.prompt: A dosa is divided into 3 equal parts. One part has spicy onion filling and two parts have plain potato filling. Draw the dosa and label each part with its fraction. Then write the fraction for the spicy onion part.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle divided into 3 equal parts; one part labelled 1/3 (spicy onion), two parts labelled 2/3 (plain potato). The fraction for the spicy onion part is 1/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the equal parts in the whole (3), then count the shaded parts (1) to write the fraction 1/3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn circle divided into 3 equal parts; stretch: ask the student to redesign the dosa so spicy onion is 2/3 and name all parts.

exercise.description: Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato; make another with 3/8 classic potato, 1/8 chilly paneer, 4/8 tangy tomato.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: Riya folds a strip of paper into two equal parts and colours one part. She then folds the strip in half again. How many equal parts does she have now? How many are coloured? Write both fractions and say whether they are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After the second fold, the strip has 4 equal parts; 2 are coloured. The two fractions are 1/2 and 2/4. They are equal — the coloured area did not change.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count all parts after each fold for the denominator, count coloured parts for the numerator; the coloured region stays the same so the fractions are equal.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a real strip and count the sections; stretch: ask what fraction they would get after one more fold and whether it is still equal to 1/2.

exercise.description: Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time; fill in: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: Arun folds a strip into three equal parts and colours one part. He folds the strip in half. He says the coloured part is now 2/6 of the strip. Is Arun correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No — folding changes the fraction, so the coloured part is now 1/6.

options.label: B
options.text: No — the coloured part became smaller when folded, so it is less than 1/3.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the coloured part is now 2/3 because you added a fold.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the strip now has 6 equal parts and 2 of them are coloured.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes — the strip now has 6 equal parts and 2 of them are coloured.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count all equal parts after the fold (6) and count coloured parts (2) to read the new fraction 2/6; the coloured area is unchanged so 1/3 = 2/6.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes the coloured region physically shrinks when the paper is folded — they are confusing the act of folding with cutting off a piece.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts only the new parts created by the fold rather than all parts in the whole strip, losing track of the denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student incorrectly doubles the numerator while keeping the denominator, misapplying the idea that folding doubles something.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fold a real strip, count all sections, and count coloured ones; stretch: ask what fraction the coloured part would be after one more fold and whether it is still equal to 1/3.

exercise.description: Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly; observe and write the fraction after each fold: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___.

items.section_title: Parts and Wholes — Halves
items.prompt: Priya folds a square piece of paper along its diagonal and says each part is one half. Her friend says the parts are not equal halves. Who is correct and how do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. A diagonal fold through the centre of a square produces two triangles of equal size. If you place one triangle on top of the other, they match exactly, so each is one half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlap the two parts to check they are the same size — if they match, each part is one half.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: invite the student to fold a paper square diagonally and overlap the two halves; stretch: ask whether a diagonal fold on a rectangle also makes equal halves, and how they would check.

exercise.description: Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen (half or two quarters) and why; try with paper; reason about equal division and Samina's choice.

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: Look at this shape: a rectangle divided into 4 parts — the top half is split into one large piece and one small piece, and the bottom half is split into one large piece and one small piece, but the pieces are unequal in size. Sana says 'The shaded top-left part is one quarter.' Is Sana correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No — the four parts are not equal in size, so no part can be called 1/4.

options.label: B
options.text: No — you need at least 8 parts to use fractions.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — as long as the whole rectangle is there, any part of 4 is called 1/4.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — there are 4 parts and one is shaded, so it is 1/4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — the four parts are not equal in size, so no part can be called 1/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether all four parts are the same size; only equal parts can be named as fractions of the whole.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student uses only the count of parts (4) to assign the fraction, ignoring the equal-size requirement — a very common preparatory-stage error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student believes that the whole's presence is sufficient to justify any fraction label, without understanding that the parts must be equal.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has formed an arbitrary rule about minimum part count that has no mathematical basis.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the rectangle and ask the student to cut and overlap the two differently sized parts to see they do not match; stretch: ask them to redraw the rectangle with the dividing lines corrected so that all four parts are equal.

exercise.description: Match the given part-shapes (hourglass, triangle, semicircle, rectangle) with their corresponding whole shapes using the 1/2 and 1/4 labels.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: Six friends share one cake equally. Later two more friends arrive and the cake is shared again equally among all eight. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Each person gets a bigger piece when there are 8 people.

options.label: B
options.text: Each person gets a smaller piece when there are 8 people.

options.label: C
options.text: Each person gets the same piece whether there are 6 or 8 people.

options.label: D
options.text: The cake gets bigger when more people share it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each person gets a smaller piece when there are 8 people.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The same whole is divided into more equal parts, so each part (1/8) is smaller than before (1/6).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is associating a larger number of people with a larger share — the most common inverse-relationship error at this stage.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student does not yet see that the number of people affects share size — they treat the share as fixed regardless of the number of people.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses sharing with the physical size of the whole object, a foundational misconception about fractions.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two circles of the same size, divide one into 6 parts and one into 8 parts, and ask which piece is bigger; stretch: ask the student to write the two fractions and explain in a sentence why one is smaller.

exercise.description: How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people? Who gets bigger pieces? Draw and explain.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: Which is greater — 1/7 or 1/4? Explain your answer without drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/4 is greater. When one whole is divided into only 4 equal parts, each part is larger than when the same whole is divided into 7 equal parts. Fewer parts means each part is bigger.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare denominators: the larger the denominator, the more parts the whole is cut into, so each part is smaller.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: allow the student to use fraction kit strips to compare 1/7 and 1/4 before writing; stretch: ask them to write a fraction that is smaller than both 1/7 and 1/4, and explain why.

exercise.description: Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4; compare 1/9 and 1/6; compare 1/6 and 1/8; choose a pair where one is smaller.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: Neha's pencil is 1/4 as long as Raj's pencil. Neha's pencil is 5 cm long. How long is Raj's pencil? Draw a line to show Raj's pencil length.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Raj's pencil is 20 cm long. If Neha's 5 cm is 1/4 of Raj's length, then Raj's pencil is 4 × 5 = 20 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If one part (1/4) equals 5 cm, multiply by 4 to find the whole: 4 × 5 = 20 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four equal boxes, write 5 cm in each, and count the total; stretch: ask what 3/4 of Raj's pencil would measure.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75
exercise.description: Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's; given Mohan's ribbon length, draw how long Rohan's ribbon would be.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: Look at a fraction chart with rows for 1/2, 1/4, 1/6, and 1/8. Pooja says: 'Two pieces of 1/4 cover the same length as one piece of 1/2.' Is Pooja correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No — two pieces of 1/4 are always shorter than one piece of 1/2.

options.label: B
options.text: No — you need three pieces of 1/4 to cover one piece of 1/2.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — but only if the pieces are from the same row of the chart.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — two pieces of 1/4 are the same length as one piece of 1/2.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes — two pieces of 1/4 are the same length as one piece of 1/2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align two 1/4 strips end to end against the 1/2 row on the fraction chart; they cover exactly the same length.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not yet grasped that 2/4 equals 1/2 and believes more pieces always mean less total length.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing 1/4 with 1/6 or miscounting the number of quarter-pieces needed to cover one half.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student understands the relationship but adds an unnecessary condition — the equivalence holds regardless of which chart row, as long as the pieces are of the whole.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place two 1/4 strips from the fraction kit next to one 1/2 strip and compare; stretch: ask how many 1/8 pieces would cover the same length as one 1/2 piece.

exercise.description: Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2; is 2/3 greater than 1/2; do ten 1/10 make a whole; do three 1/6 equal two 1/8; how many 1/8 make 1/4; find pieces that combine into a bigger piece.

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: A square is divided into 4 parts by two lines, but the parts are different sizes. Tara shades one part and writes '1/4'. What should Tara do to fix her work?

options.label: A
options.text: Change the fraction to 1/2 because she shaded one part out of four.

options.label: B
options.text: Redraw the dividing lines so all four parts are equal, then shade one part.

options.label: C
options.text: Shade one more part so two parts are shaded.

options.label: D
options.text: Write 4/1 instead of 1/4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Redraw the dividing lines so all four parts are equal, then shade one part.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction requires equal parts; fix the lines first so all four parts are the same size, then shade one to show 1/4.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focuses on the number of shaded parts and tries to match the numerator without addressing the unequal part sizes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates the count of shaded parts with a different fraction, showing confusion about what the numerator and denominator each represent.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows the fraction involves 1 and 4 but confuses the positions of numerator and denominator.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a correct and incorrect version side-by-side and ask the student to point to the one that shows 1/4; stretch: ask the student to draw two different correct ways to divide the square into 4 equal parts.

exercise.description: Bablu's squares — circle the ones cut into equal parts; write the fraction for the shaded part wherever possible.

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: Manu says: 'I shaded 3 parts of my shape, so the fraction is 3/5.' His shape has 5 equal parts. Daya says: 'I shaded 3 parts of my shape, so the fraction is 3/4.' Her shape has 4 equal parts. Who has written the correct fraction for their shading?

options.label: A
options.text: Both Manu and Daya are correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither is correct because their fractions are different.

options.label: C
options.text: Only Daya is correct.

options.label: D
options.text: Only Manu is correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both Manu and Daya are correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the shaded parts for the numerator and the total equal parts for the denominator; each has done this correctly for their own shape.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may believe that only one fraction can be correct for any shading of 3 parts, ignoring that the denominator depends on each shape's total parts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Same confusion as A but favouring Daya — the student has not recognised that the denominator comes from counting the whole shape's equal parts.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is comparing the two fractions (3/5 vs 3/4) and assuming different fractions mean one is wrong — they have not read that the shapes have different total parts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw both shapes side-by-side and ask the student to count total parts and shaded parts in each; stretch: ask which of the two fractions is greater and how they know.

exercise.description: Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims for shaded regions are correct; circle correct ones, cross out incorrect; draw lines to make parts equal if needed.

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: A square is divided into 4 equal parts. Three of the parts are shaded. Which fraction names the shaded parts?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the shaded parts (3) for the numerator and the total equal parts (4) for the denominator to write 3/4.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student writes 1/4, using only the unshaded part as the numerator — they are naming what is not shaded rather than what is.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reverses numerator and denominator, placing the count of parts on top and the number shaded below.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student writes the shaded count in both positions, confusing the role of the denominator.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: point to each part and count aloud — 'shaded: 1, 2, 3; total: 4' — then write the fraction together; stretch: ask what fraction is NOT shaded and confirm the two fractions add to 4/4.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes (diamond, rectangle, oval, L-shape, cross-shape) into 4 equal parts/quarters.

items.section_title: My Flower Garden — Non-unit Fractions
items.prompt: Draw a strip with 7 equal boxes. Colour 4 boxes yellow for sunflowers and 3 boxes pink for roses. Write the fraction of the garden that each flower covers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4/7 of the garden is sunflowers and 3/7 is roses. The two fractions together make 7/7, which is the whole garden.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the coloured boxes for each flower (numerator) and write the total number of equal boxes (7) as the denominator.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn seven-box strip; stretch: ask the student to rearrange the colours so that one flower covers more than half the garden and name that fraction.

exercise.description: Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.

items.section_title: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
items.prompt: A dosa is divided into 8 equal parts. Four parts have tomato topping, three parts have onion topping, and one part has cheese topping. What fraction of the dosa has onion topping?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the onion-topping parts (3) for the numerator; the total equal parts of the dosa (8) is the denominator, giving 3/8.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has written the fraction for the tomato topping instead of the onion topping.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has written the fraction for the cheese topping — they may have read the question as asking about the smallest portion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student uses the count of toppings (3 types) as both numerator and denominator, confusing the number of topping types with the number of equal parts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a circle divided into 8 parts and colour three of them, then count; stretch: ask the student to write the fraction for each topping and check that all three fractions add to 8/8.

exercise.book_ref: Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73
exercise.description: Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas (sectors marked with numbers show part size).

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: Draw a rectangle and divide it into 6 equal parts. Shade 4 parts to show 4/6. Now draw a circle and shade 2/3 of it. Look at both your drawings — what do you notice about the amount shaded in each?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4/6 of the rectangle and 2/3 of the circle show the same amount shaded — two-thirds of the whole in each case. Students may notice this visually even if they do not yet write the equation 4/6 = 2/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Shade 4 of 6 equal parts in the rectangle and 2 of 3 equal parts in the circle; compare the unshaded portions to see they are the same relative size.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: pre-draw the rectangle and circle and ask the student only to shade; stretch: ask the student to write a fraction equation that connects the two shadings.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: 18 mangoes are shared equally among 6 children. How many mangoes does each child get? Write the fraction that names each child's share of the whole collection.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each child gets 3 mangoes. Each child's share is 1/6 of the total collection.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total number of objects (18) by the number of equal shares (6): 18 ÷ 6 = 3; the fraction each child gets is 1/6.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 18 circles and circle them into 6 equal groups before counting; stretch: ask what fraction of the collection two children together would receive, and how many mangoes that is.

exercise.description: 12 cookies shared equally; find the fraction each child gets for 3, 6, 2, and 4 children.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: There are 20 stars. 1/4 of them are red. How many stars are red?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 stars are red. Divide 20 into 4 equal groups: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total collection (20) into 4 equal groups to find one quarter: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 20 small circles, group them into 4 equal rows, and count one row; stretch: ask how many stars are NOT red and what fraction they represent.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75
exercise.description: 16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.
